processes: Transferring electrons from a metal to a nonmetal
Building salts with repeating crystal structures
plainLanguageExplanation: An ionic bond is the bond that forms when atoms don't share — they trade. Imagine sodium, a metal that has one lonely electron in its outer shell and hates it, and chlorine, a nonmetal that needs exactly one more electron to complete its shell. When they meet, sodium hands its electron to chlorine. Now sodium is missing a negative electron, so it is positive (Na⁺), and chlorine has an extra negative electron, so it is negative (Cl⁻). And here is the magic: opposite charges attract. The positive sodium ion and negative chloride ion are pulled toward each other and lock together — that attraction is the ionic bond. Huge numbers of these ions lock together in a repeating grid called a crystal lattice — which is exactly the structure of table salt. Ionic bonds are why salt is a solid at room temperature, dissolves in water, and even conducts electricity when melted or dissolved. The key difference from a covalent bond: covalent SHARES, ionic TRANSFERS.

whyItMatters: Ionic bonds build the salts of the Earth — table salt, the minerals in rocks, the nutrients in your blood. Understanding how atoms transfer electrons explains why metals and nonmetals are such natural partners, how crystals form, and how salts conduct electricity. It is the other half of the bonding story that holds chemistry together.
didYouKnow: The salt on your table is a lattice of millions of alternating Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions — a repeating cube of positive and negative charges stacked like building blocks.
compareReason: Transferring versus sharing — comparing the ionic bond with its rival the covalent bond makes the single most important distinction in bonding crystal clear.
